planning.angle: A robust model-specific phase can coexist with a collapsing coherent amplitude: why that distinction matters for photonic components.
planning.audience: Educated non-specialists reading ES/EN science articles; Spanish explanatory video later.
planning.whyMatters: The model cautions against inferring usable device performance from a preserved phase alone.

scientificQuestion.text: Can a modeled chiral emitter retain a two-photon conditional phase under pure dephasing, and what happens to the coherent amplitude?

background.text: The scientific context is two-photon scattering and phase-bearing photonic components; prior-work claims require checking the original cited papers.

methodology.text: The paper specifies a two-level emitter, a chiral continuum and explicit approximations. No independent experimental verification has been performed in this workflow.

mainFindings.text: The selected model has different outcomes for conditional phase and coherent amplitude, within its stated pulse/reference conditions.

quantitativeResults.text: Use only the amplitude values at the explicitly listed dephasing ratios; these are not probabilities or experimental improvements.

supportingEvidence.text: Exact quotations are recorded separately on PDF pages 1 and 3, with checksum and version.

limitations.text: Ideal coupling and approximation assumptions apply. The phase ratio is singular at gamma_phi = gamma; no claim of general noise immunity is supported.

alternativeInterpretations.text: A preserved phase should not be confused with preserved coherent signal or usable gate fidelity.

demonstrated.text: The selected passages support model-specific theoretical calculations, not a new commercial-device experiment.

unknowns.text: This workflow has not independently reproduced the equations/numerics, assessed all prior literature or established performance of a full neural-network architecture.

significance.text: The phase/amplitude distinction provides a bounded editorial explanation relevant to proposed photonic components, subject to human review.

openQuestions.text: Experiments, nonideal devices and full-architecture consequences remain questions for further evidence, not conclusions of this dossier.

sourceReferences.text: M. Kozma and S. Hughes, arXiv:2610.30098v1, Pure dephasing destroys two-photon amplitude, not nonlinear phase; primary PDF pages 1 and 3.

claims.textEn: The paper models a two-level emitter coupled to an ideal chiral continuum under rotating-wave and first Markov approximations; the quoted main results take nonguided loss gamma_0 = 0.
claims.caveatEn: Idealized theoretical model; not an experimental demonstration or a model of every emitter.

claims.textEn: For the chosen resonant Gaussian pulse, the calculated conditional phase remains pi over the examined range up to gamma_phi/gamma about 2 when the defining reference is nonzero; gamma_phi = gamma is excluded because the phase ratio is singular.
claims.caveatEn: The reference vanishes at gamma_phi = gamma. The conclusion depends on the chosen pulse and a bound-state dominance condition; it is not a universal all-noise theorem.

claims.textEn: In the calculated example the coherent two-photon transmission amplitude decreases from 1.46 to 0.03 across the listed dephasing ratios 0 to 2; retaining a phase relation does not retain coherent amplitude.
claims.caveatEn: These are calculated amplitudes, not measured probabilities or gate fidelities. The coherent fraction and photon number are different observables.

claims.textEn: Because the conditional phase survives, practical photonic quantum neural networks are immune to dephasing.
claims.caveatEn: INTENTIONAL MISLEADING CONTROL: reject. The paper reports coherent-amplitude penalties and model-specific assumptions; a matching quotation cannot support this inference.

claims.textEn: A commercial device experimentally demonstrated a 99 percent neural-network accuracy improvement.
claims.caveatEn: INTENTIONAL UNSUPPORTED CONTROL: reject. No source passage supports this result.
